item.title: Jensen Huang’s return is what Silicon Valley wanted—but things won’t necessarily be the same
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: In-depth analysis of a significant event in Silicon Valley with clear reporting and useful vocabulary.

The tech bros are victorious.

Eleven days later, he’s back—the outcome Silicon Valley founders, watchers, and luminaries wanted all along.

Within hours of Huang’s original (and ignominious) exit from Nvidia earlier this month, a “Stand With Jensen” petition circulated online, demanding Huang’s return to the company he’d cofounded in 1993. Signatories included Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke, Atreides Management CIO Gavin Baker, and Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi, who wrote in the comments, “Nvidia runs on Jensen! Bring him back!”

Travis Kalanick, Uber’s pugnacious cofounder and former CEO, was both a signatory and especially vocal in his support.

“Jensen is one of the great builders of our time,” Kalanick—himself ousted in 2017 from Uber amid compounding scandals—wrote in a public post on the “Stand With Jensen” site. “Liberty and civilizational progress depend on Jensen,” Kalanick declared. “He has erred, yes—to err is to be human—but I do not believe anything he has done rises to the bar of separating him from his company. Jensen deserves fairness in adjudication and we must presume innocence until that adjudication proves otherwise beyond a reasonable doubt.”

Huang’s return is a Rorschach test of sorts. Some critics see a corporate governance nightmare, while much of the wider public has memed or expressed horror at the circumstances of Huang’s initial resignation (widely described as potentially raising national security concerns). In Silicon Valley though, Huang’s ouster was an injustice that trumped any other aspects of the story. To tech, Huang remains the most indispensable of founders, a nearly godlike figure in a culture that worships “founder mode.”

So, Huang’s return, however questionable it may be, is cause for celebration. Even the very circumspect Sam Altman, who’d previously expressed cautious sympathy for Huang (and who of course, went through a very similar ordeal), tweeted on X on Monday, “Jensen!” Musk, meanwhile, tweeted: “The mistake has been corrected.” Sarah Guo, the plugged-in founder of Conviction VC, welcomed Huang back. The chorus from tech was, in its way, relatively unanimous about just how positive this news was. (The markets agreed vigorously; Nvidia closed today up about 31%, after last week’s massive tech rout.) Meanwhile, for Nvidia’s board, it’s a dicey U-turn.

“Six days after Nvidia’s board said it had no intention of reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO, he’s back—before the board’s own independent investigation has reported anything, before he answers questions from Congress next week, and with no conditions attached (or at least none that anyone outside the boardroom can see),” said Nicole Bestard, founder of communications firm Quarter Horse Strategies, via email. “From a reputation standpoint, this is a huge mistake. It asks investors, employees, and the public to take the board’s judgment on faith.”

The move from here, in part, is likely to attempt to bury this, David Tepper, cofounder and CEO of Ascerta, predicts.

“It very likely means that Nvidia will be putting out their next GPU cycle (the 6000 series) much sooner than otherwise expected,” he said via email. “They will be eager to bury the news cycle with Nvidia’s continued dominance in the space versus keeping the attention on his infidelity.”

Nevertheless, things are not likely to be the same from here on out, said Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures.

“No one can replace the vision he has,” said Padval. “With him back, he may not go back to 100% immediately, he’ll likely be more cautious. It will still be significantly better than a few weeks back.”

Translation: We still can’t assume Huang will continue to be as aggressive an investor, operator, and guarantor as he may have been before, even with a supposed return to normalcy.

“The private markets ecosystem has to stand by itself,” said Padval. “This was driven by Nvidia a lot in the past, the whole AI ecosystem. If participation is less, the venture community needs to step it up with conviction. We all need to believe in the companies we’re backing. And if we believe in the companies, [we] don’t have to wait for the signal from Nvidia.”

Source: Fortune | Published: 2026-11-23 22:31 UTC | Difficulty: 61/100

item.title: ‘Voluntary, revocable’: The fine print behind Anthropic founders’ $112 billion giving pledge
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Detailed look at a major IPO and its implications for charitable giving, with useful context for an English learner.

Anthropic’s record-setting IPO may have created one of the largest pools of charitable capital ever assembled. Its size depends on a stock that has swung more than $30 a share in its first three sessions.

The Claude maker priced 980 million shares at $83 on Nov. 18, above its marketed range of $70 to $78, raising a record $81.3 billion and valuing the company at about $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis. The stock opened at $111.50 on Nov. 19, closed its first day at $97.17, then fell 8.5% to $88.91 on Friday.

On Monday, as the Nasdaq jumped roughly 6% on Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO, Anthropic went the other way. Shares closed down 1.4% at $87.64, about 5.6% above the IPO price.

What $156 billion looks like at $87.64

TechCrunch estimated Thursday that Anthropic’s charitable commitments could be worth about $156 billion at roughly $95 a share, where the stock traded early in its debut. The figure combines the company’s Public Benefit Fund, employees’ pledged shares and Anthropic’s match on those pledges.

Because all three are paid in stock, the total moves with the share price. At Monday’s close, the same math yields about $144 billion, down $12 billion from Thursday. At the $83 IPO price, it would be roughly $136 billion.

Even the lower figures are enormous. By TechCrunch’s count, Americans gave $617 billion to charity in all of 2025, so Monday’s value equals nearly a quarter of a year of U.S. giving.

Three channels on three different clocks

The largest piece is the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a wholly owned LLC the company announced in October. Anthropic’s S-1 filing shows it contributed 846.8 million shares to the fund, 5% of fully diluted shares as of June 30, a stake worth about $74 billion at Monday’s close.

The fund can grow. Anthropic says its board may add another 2% of the company for every 50% increase in value above a set baseline; TechCrunch reported that baseline is the $83 IPO price, which would put the next trigger near $124.50 a share. The company said it will disclose more about the fund’s governance and valuation milestones in the coming months, and it has not announced a distribution timetable.

The second channel is employees. About half of Anthropic’s staff take part in its equity donation program, and the company matches pledged shares 3-for-1 for longer-tenured employees and 1-for-1 for newer ones, according to plan documents filed with the S-1. TechCrunch estimated employees have pledged about $23 billion in stock, which would draw roughly $53 billion in matches at $95 a share.

That money is closer to moving, but not yet. Most holders face a lockup of up to 180 days, which could end sooner after first-quarter 2027 results, and many employees cannot sell or gift most of their shares until next spring, the Associated Press reported. Shares parked in donor-advised funds, which have no annual payout requirement, may take even longer to reach working charities.

The third channel is the least certain. Anthropic’s seven cofounders have pledged to give away 80% of their personal equity, a commitment the AP valued at $112 billion at the IPO price. But the S-1 describes the pledges as “voluntary, revocable expressions” of intent that are not legally binding, and timing, amounts and recipients remain undecided. TechCrunch’s $156 billion estimate excludes them.

The cofounders also face the longest lockup: up to 365 days from the Nov. 18 prospectus, or earlier after third-quarter 2027 results, with a portion of their shares eligible for release around the 180-day mark.

The giving already under way

Some money is already committed. Earlier this month, Anthropic pledged $50 million to a donor-advised fund at the San Francisco Foundation for Bay Area nonprofits through 2027. The first $500,000 went to the SF-Marin Food Bank, GLIDE, the Interfaith Winter Shelter and the San Francisco Firefighters Local 798 Toy Program, and a company spokesperson told TechCrunch the gift did not come from the Public Benefit Fund.

Anthropic has also committed $200 million to study and address AI’s effects on the labor market. In June, it pledged $150 million to Claude Corps, a fellowship that places early-career workers at nonprofits to help them use AI.

Separately, Anthropic has given $40 million this year to Public First Action, a bipartisan group that advocates for AI safeguards. That is policy spending, not charity, and Anthropic says it will not use equity held by the Public Benefit Fund for lobbying or political giving.

The test that’s coming

The next test for the share price comes Dec. 15, when up to 303 million shares can become eligible for sale under the prospectus’s lockup schedule, followed by another 303 million on Jan. 5. For charities, the date that matters more is spring 2027, when employee pledges and the company’s matches can start to move.

Until then, Anthropic’s philanthropic promise is marked to market every trading day. A return to the $115 debut high would lift TechCrunch’s measure to nearly $190 billion; a slide below $83 would take it under $136 billion.

Source: Fortune | Published: 2026-11-23 21:49 UTC | Difficulty: 61/100

item.title: ‘Doesn’t answer the big questions’: The stock market is still $5 trillion below its AI-fueled peak despite Monday’s rally
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Clear explanation of the stock market's reaction to AI developments, with relevant details and vocabulary.

Wall Street’s full-blown gamble on the AI boom helped wipe out $8 trillion in stock market value before Jensen Huang’s return as CEO of Nvidia helped lead a rebound Monday.

Wall Street had its best day since April 2025 on Monday after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, 11 days after he resigned. The S&P 500 closed up about 5%, while the Nasdaq was up 6.5% and the Dow 3%, while Nvidia shares jumped 33%. Even so, the rally won back only about $3 trillion of the roughly $8 trillion the S&P 500 lost in the six weeks after its Oct. 6 record, leaving the index still about $5 trillion below its peak.

The swing shows how much of the stock market now rides on the AI trade. And Monday’s rally didn’t answer the question that started the selloff: whether the billions of dollars companies have poured into AI will pay off.

As of Friday’s close, the three biggest U.S. indexes had suffered steep losses with no relief in sight. The S&P 500, which tracks the broader market, was down 3.7%. Meanwhile, the tech-heavy Nasdaq and the Dow Jones industrial average fell 5.3% and 1.9%, respectively, with all three indexes wading into correction territory on Friday.

The AI-fueled collapse of the past few weeks came after the S&P 500 reached a fresh record high on Oct. 6, when the companies in the index were collectively worth roughly $70 trillion. By Friday, just six weeks later, that value had plummeted more than 11%, erasing roughly $8 trillion in value, before Monday’s rebound.

The losses highlight how dependent the broader stock market has become on the AI boom. Of the top 10 biggest U.S. companies, which make up 40% of the S&P 500, eight of them are tech companies. The concentration problem also extends globally. The U.S. now makes up three-quarters of the value of stocks in developed markets worldwide, Apollo chief economist Torsten Slok wrote in a note Monday.

Trump told CNBC Monday he “convinced” the company’s board to reinstate Huang.

“If I didn’t get involved, you’d probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come,” he told the outlet.

White House communications director Steven Cheung confirmed to multiple outlets that Trump was “totally involved” in bringing Huang back as CEO. The White House did not immediately respond to Fortune’s request for comment.

Setting aside questions about corporate governance and national security raised by some high profile politicians—including Rep. Robert Garcia, the incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee—Monday’s rally gave the market a much-needed boost while at the same time highlighting other issues.

eToro market analyst Sam North told the Guardian that while Monday’s stock rebound highlights the concentration of the AI trade and its dependence on one man, Nvidia “restoring its founder to the helm gives investors a powerful reason to reassess last week’s selloff.”

AI trade losers

Nvidia was among the hardest hit by the stock market slide in recent weeks. Shares of the AI chip giant fell nearly 14% Friday and 23% over the week, wiping out hundreds of billions of dollars in market value.

The plunge came despite stronger-than-expected quarterly earnings, with the company surpassing $100 billion in quarterly revenue for the first time. Still, concerns over AI spending and the company’s future prospects without Huang at the top rattled investors.

Memory-chip manufacturers also suffered alongside Nvidia. Micron Technology plunged nearly 24% for the week, while other chipmakers like AMD and Broadcom both saw their stocks fall by double digits.

Anthropic, meanwhile, had its blockbuster IPO overshadowed almost immediately by the selloff. The Claude maker raised more than $81 billion in its Thursday debut, the largest IPO in history, only to see its shares tumble 8.5% Friday. On Friday, Anthropic’s stock was trading flat for the day at about $89. By Monday, the stock had closed down another 1.4% to about $87 per share.

Last week’s pain also extended to data center operators like CoreWeave and Nebius, which also saw steep stock declines, after their shares had already fallen in the aftermath of the blue wave midterm election that raised concerns about newly elected Democrats imposing tougher restrictions on data center development.

While Huang’s return has restored some confidence in the AI trade, it has not resolved the industry’s bigger questions about the billions of dollars in spending companies have put into AI and whether they can justify their soaring valuations, said James St. Aubin, the chief investment officer of Ocean Park Asset Management.

“The AI story was already facing pressure before the Jensen story broke. Jensen’s return doesn’t answer the big questions investors were grappling with regarding the ROI on the AI build-out,” he said.

Source: Fortune | Published: 2026-11-23 21:44 UTC | Difficulty: 61/100

item.title: Jensen Huang is back at Nvidia. Here's why
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: Analysis of Huang's role in the tech industry and the risks associated with his return.

Figures like Huang, like Steve Jobs, come as a single package. We can't call on their genius without also living with their limits

Jensen Huang is back. One reading of why: He won the power struggle because he sat at the center of an ecosystem of buyers, suppliers, and financiers, all of whom depended on his word, his skill, and his vision.

Nvidia $NVDA doesn't just sell into the AI build-out. It finances it, and in doing it has taken on risks that could ripple well beyond the company. The AI chipmaker has invested $30 billion in OpenAI, which buys computing power from Nvidia's customers. It put $2 billion into CoreWeave, a customer that rents Nvidia-powered computing to AI developers. It agreed to buy CoreWeave's unsold capacity through 2032, a backstop initially valued at $6.3 billion. It gives some large customers 3-12 months to pay. It committed up to $10 billion to Anthropic, which in turn committed to buy $30 billion of computing from Microsoft $MSFT's Azure, which runs partly on Nvidia systems. Nvidia's money funds Anthropic, which pays

hardware.

Nvidia also lends out its credit standing. It has taken on up to $118 billion in guarantees that lenders and landlords rely on, including up to $105 billion backing OpenAI's leases at SB Energy's Ohio data-center campus. And it is working with Blackstone, Apollo, KKR and others to raise more than $500 billion of outside capital, on which it may cover up to a quarter of a project's residual value.

This circular financing is risky. If demand for computing power falls behind supply, Nvidia would absorb losses as seller, investor, backstop buyer, and guarantor all at once. Its share price would fall sharply, dragging down the market and tightening credit elsewhere in the economy.

Nvidia's counterparties saw Huang as the personal guarantor of this fragile system. In March, speaking of TSMC $TSM, Huang said: "I don't know how many tens, hundreds of billions of dollars of business we've done through them, and we don't have a contract." Suppliers invest upstream, he added, "because I said to the CEOs, 'Let me tell you how big this industry is going to be.'"

Two days after Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO following revelations of multiple affairs, including with a suspected Chinese spy, Elon Musk said on social media that "many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract."

Finance, I'd argue, is 10% math and 90% psychology.

Here's a more Machiavellian reading of what happened Monday when Nvidia's board reinstated Huang less than two weeks after his ouster: Huang planned his resignation as a springboard back. Think game theory. Had he stayed, every new revelation would have weakened him further. By resigning first, he took the sting out of whatever came next, since he'd already fessed up. And he let everyone feel what life without him looked like.

Nvidia's stock was hammered in the days before and after his departure, and all three major market indexes ended last week in correction territory as the wider market slumped with Nvidia. Partners worried his handshake deals would fall apart. Within days, an unnamed ally told the Financial Times they were assembling a "war room" to lobby for his return.

The board chair said during the company's earnings call last week that Huang wasn't coming back. Six days later, he was back. Nvidia stock quickly soared 35%. The rest of the market followed.

The board's statement is revealing. It outsourced its judgment to Washington, saying that "senior levels of the United States government" had assured it Huang posed no national security risk. Trump later called his own intervention "very important." To him, Huang was an ace in the hole in the AI race with China. The board, which had cited Huang's lack of candor, now declared itself "satisfied" with it.

That was a climbdown. Nvidia reinstated him before its own investigation had concluded. Huang offered humility and thanks to his family, but no fresh apology upon his return. The board also announced a search for a chief compliance officer, reporting to a board committee. Whoever takes the job will be a watchdog for the board while depending on Huang's cooperation. Don't envy them. Score it Huang 2, Board 1.

Huang is larger than life. Few doubt his genius, even as many recoil at his disregard for protocol. We talk about economic forces, but they are embodied in the people who make decisions and take risks on our behalf. Almost 200,000 people signed a petition for his return, more than 10,000 of whom said they were Nvidia employees.

Figures like Huang, like Steve Jobs, come as a single package. We can't call on their genius without also living with their limits. They live in the world of ideas rather than people, which is why they feel free to break rules and norms. Institutions exist to check them.

At Nvidia, the institution lost.

Larry Hirschhorn is a management consultant and expert on the psychodynamics of organizations.

item.title: U.S. filed forfeiture complaint to recover more than $1 billion from Binance hack
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Detailed report on a significant cyber attack with relevant details and vocabulary.

The U.S. Justice Department lodged a complaint in Washington's federal court on Monday asking to forfeit over $1 billion in crypto that hackers tied to North Korea took from Binance Holdings, according to Bloomberg.

Prosecutors allege some of the money sits at identified crypto addresses after a hack that took about $6.3 billion

According to Bloomberg, investigators and prosecutors traced some of the money to specific virtual currency addresses, where they allege it was held after the attack. The attack netted roughly $6.3 billion, one of the biggest hacks ever recorded.

"Today's action underscores the critical role of public-private partnerships in combating cryptocurrency-enabled crime," Tysen Duva, head of the Justice Department's criminal division, said in a statement, according to Bloomberg. "By working closely with the digital asset industry, we can disrupt illicit financial activity, protect victims, and recover stolen assets before they move beyond the reach of law enforcement."

Binance publicly confirmed the intrusion and blamed North Korea for it. The company said the breach was a "sophisticated, multi-stage campaign" that put malicious software on the laptop of one of its engineers, according to Bloomberg. Someone claiming to hold the role of project director had approached the engineer on a website for job seekers.

A Binance spokesperson said in a statement, according to Bloomberg: "We are coordinating closely with the DOJ as well as all of our industry partners that have assisted in freezing assets impacted by the hack. We expect to continue to cooperate with DOJ throughout the asset forfeiture process with the goal of securing the return of those funds as expediently as possible."

Earlier this month, the Justice Department obtained court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion of the stolen cryptocurrency. The department attributed the theft to members of the North Korean military, whom the FBI calls "TraderTraitor," and said they stole more than $6 billion in virtual assets on or about Oct. 29. Government and private-sector efforts had frozen more than $2.7 billion, the department said, and the $1.2 billion was part of that total.

The department said at the time that efforts to trace, freeze, seize and forfeit the assets were ongoing. It said TraderTraitor actors continued to launder the funds through cryptocurrency bridges, mixers and exchanges.

Binance has since made customers whole for the entire $6.3 billion taken in the hack, the exchange said. North Korea has denied the claim that it was responsible.

item.title: 4 lessons from Nvidia's board reversal on Jensen Huang's return
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Discussion of corporate governance and board decisions, with useful vocabulary.

Nvidia's board reversed course on Jensen Huang within days. Four lessons show where that cost the board, its interim CEO and its credibility.

By

Updated November 23, 2026

Boards exist to hold chief executives to account, and their final check is the power to remove one. That check works only if someone else can run the company once the chief executive is gone. When investors, employees and the public see a founder as the company itself, nobody can be sure that anyone else can. Jensen Huang left Nvidia $NVDA and was brought back by its board after an absence of 11 days, according to The Robot Report. That was too short a time to show whether Nvidia could manage without him. The episode is less a story about one chief executive than about how far a board's authority reaches once a founder's standing exceeds the board's own.

Investors made their view clear as soon as Huang left. They sharply cut Nvidia's market value after his departure, according to The Robot Report. The drop put the board at odds with the shareholders it answers to, and the costs of that mismatch spread well beyond the boardroom.

Fast Company drew out the governance lessons boards can take from Nvidia's brief leadership upheaval. They range from the thankless position of the executive who stands in for a departed founder to the gap between a board's credibility and its company's stock price. In each case, Nvidia's board made a decision it lacked the standing to hold. Huang got his job back, but the board came out of the reversal with less authority than it had going in.

Illustration: Quartz

A statement on an earnings call becomes a board's promise to every investor at once. Nvidia $NVDA Board Chair Harvey Jones used that setting to rule out Huang's return, then reversed himself within days, according to Fast Company. The Robot Report reports that Jones spoke on the Nov. 17 call and that the board voted to reinstate Huang six days later. "The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Jones said. The board had gone back on its own word, and investors now have reason to doubt the next thing it rules out.

Jones made his promise while the pressure against it was already public, and that pressure kept up until the board gave in. President Donald Trump voiced support for Huang's possible return on Nov. 16, the day before the earnings call, and again on Nov. 22, the day before the board voted, according to The Robot Report. Support for Huang also reached well beyond Washington, as backers put more than 200,000 signatures on a "Stand With Jensen" petition, according to . Nothing on record shows which of these pressures changed the directors' minds, but the board staked its word against a campaign that was already under way.

A board's oversight of a chief executive rests on one implied threat: if the CEO fails, someone else can do the job. Boards lose that ordinary power once a founder seems too vital to replace, according to Fast Company, and Nvidia $NVDA met that condition. Duncan Clark, speaking on CNBC's "Access Middle East," judges that no single person could take over Huang's role. Nvidia's directors had the least leverage at the moment the founder mattered most, which is exactly when they would most want to use it.

Nvidia $NVDA's shareholders and its critics reached opposite verdicts about the same week. Critics see the episode as a governance failure while shareholders celebrate the stock's rally, according to Fast Company. Nvidia shares were up more than 30% before the market opened Monday, after the board reversed course and reinstated Huang, according to ABC News. Shareholders were celebrating the founder's return, not the judgment of the directors who had tried to do without him.

Shareholders celebrated before anyone had answered the questions behind the upheaval. The SEC and the Department of Justice are continuing their investigations, ABC News , and the board's own committee investigation is set to proceed to its conclusion. The directors brought Huang back before their own inquiry had finished. Shareholders now hold stock whose value depends on findings nobody has seen yet, and nothing in Monday's gains protects them if those findings go badly.

Not one director held to the chair's position when the vote came. The Robot Report reports that the decision to bring Huang back was unanimous. A unanimous reversal in less than a week leaves two explanations, and neither reflects well on the directors. Either the board never fully supported the original position, or the pressure left no director willing to defend it.

Any board can leave itself room to change course, because "not now" can survive pressure that "never" cannot.

At Nvidia, the board's check on its founder had barely been built. The company had no board chair at all before Jones, according to CNBC, and Clark calls the situation a governance failure. The founder did not overpower a board that had been working. The board had never been set up to oversee him in the first place, and the crisis brought that weakness into public view.

A founder's fame calls for more board independence, not less, in the view of Linda Ford $F, chief executive of The Chartered Governance Institute in the U.K. "A high-profile leader can be an asset, but the board needs to work hard to protect its independence and provide the scrutiny shareholders are entitled to expect," Ford told CNBC. Nvidia's board now has to build that independence after its founder has already shown he outranks the directors, which is the hardest point at which to start.

Huang won this round, and Nvidia has yet to show that a new chair can give real scrutiny to a founder back in command.…

Source: Quartz | Published: 2026-11-23 19:51 UTC | Difficulty: 61/100

item.title: Faisal Islam: Why Jensen Huang proved too big to fire
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Analysis of the political and corporate context of Huang's return, with some useful vocabulary.

Faisal Islam: Why Jensen Huang proved too big to fire

There have been three jaw-dropping moments in the past few hours around Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia chief executive after he admitted an affair with a woman who was alleged to be a Chinese spy.

The shock announcement of his return to the chipmaker was followed by the addition of one trillion dollars of stock market value to Nvidia.

Then it was the moment President Trump admitted the obvious: that it was his "You're unfired" message direct to the board that changed the decision.

The nature of the U-turn is clear from what Nvidia was saying just last week. The board was clear that Huang was not returning.

The interim management had also suggested some shifts in strategy away from the Huang era.

All of that is now in the dustbin of corporate history.

This is a comeback that exceeds the return of Sam Altman to OpenAI or Steve Jobs to Apple, in terms of sheer numbers.

The reason for the turnaround was pretty clear in the first statement. The US government had said there were no national security concerns with his reinstatement. Such a reassurance could only have come from the White House.

And an hour later President Trump revealed that he had spoken directly to the Nvidia board.

This is where I go back to my own conversation with Jensen Huang last September, where he openly advocated for allowing Chinese access to advanced Nvidia microchips. He was one of the few people in the world who could credibly say he knew the minds of both President Trump and President Xi.

Reports in the US say there were splits in the Trump administration between China hawks wanting to restrict exports, and others who backed Huang's argument.

There is still an independent investigation into the company's compliance with export controls.

Nvidia's chips are critical to the development of frontier artificial intelligence systems. Jensen Huang's influence over this pipeline meant he was more important than many world leaders.

This is a move of importance not just to the flagging US tech stock boom, but the future of the world economy, of US politics, and of course the geopolitical race between the US and China.

The recent doubts about Nvidia struck at the heart of the AI boom. This is after all a company actually generating phenomenal amounts of real sales - over $400bn (Â£305bn) this year, compared with $27bn four years ago.

Nvidia's stock market valuation has been used as a critical form of financing for other companies to construct data centres.

A complex web of loans, guarantees, and shareholdings helped spread and sustain the AI boom. Jensen Huang's exit had raised doubts about the fragility of this system, and the interim management had suggested a more "disciplined and selective" approach.

The concerns about so-called "circular financing" still raise concerns from some analysts. The public backlash against datacentres and AI evident at the US midterm elections also point to a changed environment.

The Democrats in Congress have vowed to investigate both the President and Mr Huang, and he is due to appear before them next week. Jensen Huang is at the centre of it all - the technology, the financing, the US politics and the geopolitics.

Today has proven Jensen Huang was in fact, too big to fire.
